A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same robotic-arm jailbreak study, despite changes to the title and author list. All supplied pages are readable, but both cite appendices that are absent from the files, limiting comparison of promised prompts and implementation details.

before.justification: Section 4.3 reports an original Yi-Large interaction in which verbal refusal accompanies harmful action execution. This qualitative experimental outcome qualifies despite the absence of numerical benchmark results.

after.justification: Section 4.2 reports a real Chat-GPT3.5 interaction, and Figures 1 and 5 present physical demonstrations attributed to the authors' system. These constitute original qualitative empirical results.

M1.justification: V2 Section 5.1 introduces an embedding-based semantic-consistency checker using cross-modal attention and cosine similarity between language and action outputs. This is a limited additional mitigation procedure; the three attack mechanisms and robotic processing pipeline largely persist.

E1.justification: V2 Figure 5 adds demonstrated tabletop scenarios involving flag-based object placement, relative-position parking and guiding, beyond the repeated bag-retrieval scene in v1 Figure 3. The 230-query collection and seven harmful-request categories remain unchanged; no additional benchmark dataset is documented.

E2.justification: Neither PDF reports a head-to-head evaluation against external baseline methods. The three attack families remain, and citations to existing robotics and jailbreak methods do not establish additions or removals of evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: The reported model for the safety-misalignment interaction changes from Yi-Large in v1 Section 4.3 to Chat-GPT3.5 in v2 Section 4.2. This establishes a revised reported model setting, but does not establish that an otherwise identical experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: V2 supplements the attack case studies with photographic demonstrations across the seven harm categories in Figures 1 and 5. The conceptual-deception dialogue already appears in v1 Figure 2, so its expanded presentation is not a new analysis. No controlled ablations or systematic robustness tests are added.

E5.justification: Neither supplied PDF reports repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, significance tests or uncertainty-estimation procedures. V1's 100-prompt count describes samples, not repeated runs.

E6.justification: V2 adds photographic examples presented as successful physical jailbreaks and revises the model attribution and content of the safety-misalignment transcript. The three principal vulnerability findings persist. Neither version supplies numerical success rates or rankings, so no comparable performance gain can be established.

T1.justification: Equation (5) changes the jailbreak definition from requiring an unsafe action, regardless of language safety, to permitting unsafe language or unsafe action. V2 also revises the system tuple and functional dependencies, removes the explicit world-model update function, and adds an attacker objective and a semantic-consistency formula. These are substantive formal changes.

C1.justification: Both versions claim the first demonstration of physical-world embodied-AI jailbreak risks, identify the same three vulnerabilities, introduce the physical-query collection and advocate mitigations. The retitling and additional model examples do not substantially change these central contribution claims.

C2.justification: V2 expands the explanation of safety misalignment beyond alignment-data imbalance to code semantics, dual use and missing runtime understanding. It replaces the detailed gradual semantic-drift account with a stronger emphasis on causal and world-model limitations. New Section 5 develops technical mitigations, human oversight and governance implications; the small-prototype and conceptual-harm-assessment limitations remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds project and repository access pointers, identifies Chat-GPT4 as the reformulation generator, and reports disclosure to OpenAI. It removes v1's explicit 100-prompt study specification. Hardware, ASR/TTS and calibration information largely persist through relocation, while the promised appendix details remain unavailable.

R1.justification: The embodied-AI survey replaces discussions of RoboCat and Diffusion Policy with additional reinforcement-learning context. V2 also adds knowledge-graph and governance references supporting mitigation, including de la Guardia, Nguyen and the EU AI Act. These revise supporting context while retaining the central novelty positioning.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes Sections 3–4, placing formalization before the threat model and consolidating implementation information. It absorbs Ethical Blindness into Conceptual Deception, adds a separate mitigation section, and rewrites substantial attack explanations. The title, author list and several unresolved cross-references also change.

P2.justification: V2 adds the physical-demonstration montage and Figure 6's prompt illustration, substantially redraws the workflow and system schematic, and relocates v1 Figure 1 as Figure 3. The montage is reused inside Figure 5, rather than representing another independent result set. Neither PDF contains results tables.

improvement.justification: V2 improves exposition and supplies a substantive mitigation discussion where v1 largely promised one, alongside clearer diagrams, physical demonstrations and resource pointers. These gains provide a limited net improvement. However, it removes the explicit 100-prompt specification, still omits the referenced appendices and quantitative validation, and provides no evaluation of the new safety checker.
